How large a sample do you need?

Source: R/plan.R
plan_size.Rd

Solves for n given the precision you want, rather than asking you to guess it. This is the step before draw(): you rarely know the sample size, you know the margin of error you can live with.

Usage

plan_size(
  margin,
  sd = NULL,
  p = 0.5,
  N = Inf,
  level = 0.95,
  deff = 1,
  response = 1,
  target = c("mean", "proportion", "total"),
  strata = NULL,
  allocation = c("proportional", "equal", "neyman"),
  min_per_stratum = 2L
)

Arguments

margin

Half-width of the confidence interval you want, the half-width the plan expects (see "Where the formula comes from"). For a proportion it is a proportion, and a margin of 1 or more is refused. Several margins give several plans (see "Several plans at once").

sd

Standard deviation of the measure, for target = "mean" or "total", as stats::sd() computes it. Not used with strata.

p

Expected proportion, for target = "proportion". Not used with strata.

N

Population size, at least 1. Inf for an effectively unbounded frame. An estimated N need not be a whole number; n is at most floor(N). Not used with strata, whose sizes add up to it.

level

Confidence level.

deff

Design effect to inflate by: a positive number, or the result of ht_mean() for a mean or a proportion, or of ht_total() for a total, on a pilot sample. 1 assumes simple random sampling. A number should come from deff() on the estimator you will report, rounded up, or from deff_cluster() (see "The corrections"). With strata it inflates the variance of the stratified sample, as for clusters sampled within strata.

response

Expected response rate, between 0 and 1.

target

"mean", "proportion" or "total". For "total" the margin is on the population total and N must be finite.

strata

NULL, or a data frame with a row per stratum, to plan a stratified sample (see "Planning a stratified sample"). Its columns are those that name the strata; N, the rows of the frame in each stratum; sd, the standard deviation of the measure within each stratum, or for a proportion p, the expected proportion within it; and, with allocation = "neyman" only, an optional cost, the cost of one row in each stratum.

allocation

How n is split over strata: "proportional", "equal" or "neyman", as in design_stratified(). Neyman shares are proportional to N_h * S_h, or N_h * S_h / sqrt(cost_h) with a cost column.

min_per_stratum

The fewest rows a stratum is allocated, as in design_stratified(), 1 or more. A stratum smaller than this is taken whole. The default of 2 is the fewest that give each stratum a variance, which ht_total() and ht_mean() need from every stratum not taken whole. 0, the default of design_stratified(), is refused, since a split without a floor can leave a small stratum without rows, and the estimate then leaves it out.

Value

A plan, a list of class drawn_plan with a print() method, or for several plans a data frame (see "Several plans at once"). A plan holds:

n

Draw this many. Never more than N, and without strata at least two when the frame has two rows or more.

n_effective

What you expect to analyse once response has taken its share.

capped

TRUE when only a census meets the margin, so n is every row of the frame. A census meets any margin when everyone responds.

short

TRUE when a sample smaller than the frame would meet the margin if everyone responded, but not at this response rate, so n is the whole frame and the margin achieved will be wider than the one asked for. It is never TRUE with capped.

raised

TRUE when the margin alone needs one row, and n_effective was raised to two, the fewest that give a standard error and an interval.

margin, level, N, deff, response, target

The inputs, returned so the assumptions travel with the number. deff is the number used, also when an estimate was passed.

p

The expected proportion for a proportion, and NA for a mean or a total.

n_needed

Rows that would reach the margin if everyone responded, two at least as for n_effective. Equal to n_effective unless the whole frame is drawn at a response below 1.

spread

The standard deviation used, sd, or sqrt(p * (1 - p)) for a proportion. NA with strata.

With strata there are four more, and raised is always FALSE, since min_per_stratum sets the floor:

allocation

The rows to draw from each stratum, a data frame of the strata columns and n, in the order of strata. Pass it to design_stratified() as allocation to draw that split.

strata

The strata as given, checked, with n added.

rule, min_per_stratum

The allocation rule and the floor used.

A plan can be passed as n to any design that takes n, such as design_simple(n = plan), which draws plan$n rows. as.data.frame() turns it into a data frame of one row, with a column for each field above, except that a stratified plan has the number of strata in place of the two data frames. Several plans at once give a data frame of those rows, one per plan.

What you need to supply

A margin of error, and some idea of how much the thing you are measuring varies:

  • For a mean or total, an sd — from a pilot, last year's data, or a range divided by four as a rough stand-in.

  • For a proportion, a p. Leave it at 0.5, the most pessimistic value, unless you have a better guess; that is the honest default because it maximises the required size. The margin is a proportion too, 0.03 for 3 percentage points.

sd given for a proportion, or p for a mean or a total, is not used, and plan_size() warns that it is ignored.

For a stratified sample, give the size and the spread of each stratum in strata instead (see "Planning a stratified sample").

The corrections

N applies a finite population correction: sampling 400 from 500 is very different from 400 from 500,000, and past a certain point a bigger frame stops mattering. response inflates for non-response: at 0.6 you draw enough to end up with what you need.

deff inflates for the design, since a clustered design of 400 may carry the information of 100. Before any pilot, deff_cluster() gives the design effect of taking m rows from each cluster from their intraclass correlation. Measure it with deff() on a comparable past sample, using the estimator you will report: ht_mean() for a mean or a proportion, and ht_total() for a total. The two design effects differ for the same sample, and can differ many times over. In one cluster sample with clusters of 2 to 40 rows, the total's design effect was 28 and the mean's 0.66, and a total planned with the mean's figure came out a small fraction of the size it needed. A total reported as N times a mean takes the mean's design effect, and is planned as a mean with margin / N. You can pass the result of ht_mean() or ht_total() itself as deff, and plan_size() refuses one of the wrong kind for target.

A design effect from one pilot is an estimate, and a noisy one, which comes out below the truth more often than above it. Round it up. deff() gives NA for a pilot without a variance estimate, such as one taken with variance = "none", a census, or one with a single cluster, and for one in which y took a single value. It is NA too for a mean from ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) with y missing in some sampled rows, since the rows with y are a domain, whose design effect is not estimated. Such a pilot cannot supply a design effect, and plan_size() refuses an NA. It refuses an estimate from survey too, such as survey::svymean(deff = TRUE), whose value is the estimate itself; pass survey::deff() of it instead.

Planning a stratified sample

With strata, plan_size() plans a stratified simple random sample, as design_stratified() draws one. For each total n it splits n over the strata as that design would, by the same allocation rule, the floor min_per_stratum and largest-remainder rounding, with no stratum given more rows than it has, and works out the variance of the stratified mean, deff * sum(W_h^2 * (1 / n_h - 1 / N_h) * S_h^2) with W_h = N_h / N (Cochran 1977, chapter 5). For a proportion S_h^2 is N_h * p_h * (1 - p_h) / (N_h - 1). The plan is the smallest n whose variance is at most (margin / z)^2, with margin / N for a total. min_per_stratum must be 1 or more, since an estimate leaves a stratum without rows out. Without a floor, proportional allocation gives a stratum of one row in a frame of 200,000 its first row at n of about 100,000, and the plan would be that large. The rounded split can take a row from one stratum as n grows, so the variance does not always fall with n, and the search checks each n from the first that could meet the margin.

response divides n as without strata, and the rows to draw are split by the same rule. The split is returned as allocation, which design_stratified() takes as the count for each stratum. Passing the plan as n instead lets the design split n again by its own rule and min_per_stratum, whose default there is 0, which can leave a small stratum without rows.

Several plans at once

margin, sd, p, deff and response each take one value, or several for several plans. Those with one value are used for every plan, and those with several must have the same number, one per plan, so plan_size(margin = c(3, 5, 10), sd = 40) plans three margins at the same spread. The result is then a data frame with a row per plan, as as.data.frame() gives for each, without the split over strata or the printed notes.

Where the formula comes from

n0 = (z * spread / margin)^2 * deff is the size for an unbounded frame, with z the normal quantile for level and, for a total, margin / N as the margin on the mean. For a mean or a total the finite population correction gives n0 / (1 + n0 / N), the smallest n with (1 / n - 1 / N) * deff * sd^2 <= (margin / z)^2. For a proportion, whose variance p * (1 - p) has the divisor N rather than N - 1, it gives n0 / (1 + (n0 - 1) / N). The result is rounded up, raised to two when it is one, and divided by response (Cochran 1977, chapter 4; Valliant, Dever and Kreuter 2018, chapter 3).

margin is the half-width the plan expects, the usual convention for sizing a sample: the estimate from a sample of size n lands within margin of the truth with probability about level. The interval a sample reports is built from that sample's own estimate of the variance, which comes out above the planned variance about as often as below it, so the reported half-width is wider than margin about half the time.

That interval also uses t on the design's degrees of freedom rather than z, which matters when the primary sampling units are few. With 3, 4 and 6 clusters in one stratum, which give 2, 3 and 5 degrees of freedom, the 95% t quantile is 2.2, 1.6 and 1.3 times z. plan_size() counts rows and knows nothing of clusters, so when you turn n into a few clusters, plan more of them.

For a proportion, ht_mean() reports an interval on the logit scale, which is asymmetric. When p is small its upper arm is longer than its lower one, and exceeds margin in most samples even when the estimate is as precise as planned.

References

Cochran, W. G. (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd ed. Wiley.

Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. Wiley.

Valliant, R., Dever, J. A. and Kreuter, F. (2018). Practical Tools for Designing and Weighting Survey Samples, 2nd ed. Springer.

See also

deff() to measure the design effect of a past sample, deff_cluster() for one from an intraclass correlation, draw() to take the sample.

Examples

# A proportion, no prior guess, 20,000 in the frame
plan_size(margin = 0.03, N = 20000, target = "proportion")
#> Sample size for a proportion
#>   draw           1,014
#>   margin         +/- 0.03 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       p 0.5, N 20,000

# A mean, when a pilot put the spread near 40
plan_size(margin = 5, sd = 40, N = 20000)
#> Sample size for a mean
#>   draw           243
#>   margin         +/- 5 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       sd 40, N 20,000

# The same, in a clustered design with 70% response
plan_size(margin = 5, sd = 40, N = 20000, deff = 2.5, response = 0.7)
#> Sample size for a mean
#>   draw           853
#>   to analyse     597  (after 70% response)
#>   margin         +/- 5 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       sd 40, deff 2.5, N 20,000

# A total, to within 100,000 across a 20,000-row frame
plan_size(margin = 1e5, sd = 40, N = 20000, target = "total")
#> Sample size for a total
#>   draw           243
#>   margin         +/- 100,000 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       sd 40, N 20,000

# Clusters of ten rows, whose rows correlate at 0.05, before any pilot
plan_size(margin = 5, sd = 40, N = 20000,
          deff = deff_cluster(m = 10, icc = 0.05))
#> Sample size for a mean
#>   draw           351
#>   margin         +/- 5 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       sd 40, deff 1.45, N 20,000

# Three margins at once, one plan per row
plan_size(margin = c(3, 5, 10), sd = 40, N = 20000)
#>     n n_effective margin level     N deff response target spread  p capped
#> 1 661         661      3  0.95 20000    1        1   mean     40 NA  FALSE
#> 2 243         243      5  0.95 20000    1        1   mean     40 NA  FALSE
#> 3  62          62     10  0.95 20000    1        1   mean     40 NA  FALSE
#>   short raised n_needed
#> 1 FALSE  FALSE      661
#> 2 FALSE  FALSE      243
#> 3 FALSE  FALSE       62

# A plan is a valid `n`
design_simple(n = plan_size(margin = 5, sd = 40, N = 20000))
#> <sampling design: simple>
#>   n        243
#>   replace  FALSE
#>   reserve  0

# Three strata, with the spread of each from an earlier survey
bands <- data.frame(band = c("small", "medium", "large"),
                    N = c(1200, 600, 200), sd = c(10, 25, 80))
plan <- plan_size(margin = 2, strata = bands, allocation = "neyman")
plan
#> Sample size for a mean, over 3 strata
#>   draw           312
#>   margin         +/- 2 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       Neyman allocation, at least 2 rows per stratum, N 2,000
#> 
#>        band    N sd   n
#>       small 1200 10  87
#>      medium  600 25 109
#>       large  200 80 116
frame <- data.frame(id = 1:2000,
                    band = rep(bands$band, times = bands$N))
s <- draw(frame, design_stratified("band", allocation = plan$allocation),
          seed = 1)
table(s$band)
#> 
#>  large medium  small 
#>    116    109     87 

# The design effect of a cluster pilot, passed as the estimate itself
pop <- data.frame(cl = rep(paste0("c", 1:50), each = 8))
pop$y <- rep(seq(10, 59), each = 8) + rep(c(-3, 3), 200)
pilot <- draw(pop, design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 6), seed = 1,
              weights = TRUE)
plan_size(margin = 3, sd = sd(pilot$y), N = nrow(pop),
          deff = ht_mean(pilot, "y"))
#> Sample size for a mean
#>   draw           294
#>   margin         +/- 3 at 95% confidence
#>   assuming       sd 16.86, deff 9.1, N 400
